title: The Bank That Toppled a President

lines.text: At 3:24 in the morning on November 2nd, 2026, Paraguay's central bank posted a short message online.
lines.say: At three twenty-four in the morning on November second, 2026, Paraguay's central bank posted a short message online.

lines.text: By sunrise, the most popular banking app in the country had stopped working.

lines: Three million customers, about six in ten adults, could not pay, withdraw cash, or use their cards.

lines.text: Five days later, the President of Paraguay was out of office and under arrest.

lines: How does one bank bring down a president?

lines.text: Ueno started in 1976 as a small finance company, and for decades almost nobody noticed it.
lines.say: Wenno started in 1976 as a small finance company, and for decades almost nobody noticed it.

lines.text: In 2021 a powerful business family, Grupo Vázquez, took control, renamed it Ueno, and turned it into an app.
lines.say: In 2021 a powerful business family, Groopo Vasquez, took control, renamed it Wenno, and turned it into an app.

lines: It offered cashback on groceries, credit cards for people who had never had one, and its name on the shirts of the national football team.
In 2023 it won a full banking licence. In 2024 it bought another bank, Visión Banco, and became the sixth-largest bank in the country.

lines.text: At the same time, Paraguay was selling itself to investors as the "Dubai of South America": low taxes, steady growth, and new investment-grade credit ratings.
lines.say: At the same time, Paraguay was selling itself to investors as the Dubai of South America. Low taxes, steady growth, and new investment-grade credit ratings.

lines.text: Paraguay's president, Santiago Peña, was a former IMF economist elected in 2023.
lines.say: Paraguay's president, Santiago Penya, was a former I.M.F. economist elected in 2023.

lines.text: Before and during his presidency, he held a small stake in Ueno's holding company. He said he sold it in 2025.
lines.say: Before and during his presidency, he held a small stake in Wenno's holding company. He said he sold it in 2025.

lines.text: He also picked Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno's predecessor company, to run the central bank: the regulator that was supposed to watch Ueno.
lines.say: He also picked Carlos Carvayo, who had led Wenno's predecessor company, to run the central bank. The regulator that was supposed to watch Wenno.

lines.text: And public money poured in. By August 2026, state agencies had about 850 million dollars at Ueno, including around 355 million from the national social security fund.
lines.say: And public money poured in. By August 2026, state agencies had about 850 million dollars at Wenno, including around 355 million from the national social security fund.

lines: Paraguay's social security institute had loosened its own rules, which let it put more of its money there.
In June 2026, central bank inspectors flagged about 146 million dollars in risky loans to companies linked to the bank's own owners.

lines.text: That summer, the newspaper ABC Color started asking questions. Ueno threatened to sue.
lines.say: That summer, the newspaper A.B.C. Color started asking questions. Wenno threatened to sue.

lines.text: In October, a leaked central bank report naming problems at Ueno reached the Senate. Peña criticised the leak, and Ueno questioned whether the document was genuine.
lines.say: In October, a leaked central bank report naming problems at Wenno reached the Senate. Penya criticised the leak, and Wenno questioned whether the document was genuine.

lines.text: On paper, Ueno said it was healthy, with capital above the legal minimum. On October 30th, it announced a plan to raise 100 million dollars.
lines.say: On paper, Wenno said it was healthy, with capital above the legal minimum. On October thirtieth, it announced a plan to raise 100 million dollars.

lines: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this story and haven't subscribed yet, tap subscribe.

lines.text: Three days later, the central bank shut it down.
Inspectors said that once bad loans were counted properly, Ueno's capital was not 13.8 percent. It was 5.56 percent, less than half the legal minimum.
lines.say: Inspectors said that once bad loans were counted properly, Wenno's capital was not thirteen point eight percent. It was five point five six percent. Less than half the legal minimum.

lines: Overnight, millions of accounts froze. Salaries, savings and pensions were stuck.
Shops lost their payment systems. In some cities, a school meals programme was suspended.

lines.text: A state guarantee fund began paying depositors back. Officials said 97 percent of customers would be covered in full, but Moody's estimated only about a third of the money held at the bank was insured.
lines.say: A state guarantee fund began paying depositors back. Officials said ninety-seven percent of customers would be covered in full. But Moody's estimated only about a third of the money held at the bank was insured.

lines.text: Paraguay's currency fell more than 8 percent against the dollar.
lines.say: Paraguay's currency fell more than eight percent against the dollar.

lines: Monday, November 3rd: the central bank chief resigned. Crowds gathered outside closed branches.

lines.text: Then the crowds moved to Congress and the president's residence. Ueno's own staff burned their company cards. Police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets.
lines.say: Then the crowds moved to Congress and the president's residence. Wenno's own staff burned their company cards. Police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets.

lines.text: Thursday, November 5th: Peña said he would resign "for the stability of our country."
lines.say: Thursday, November fifth. Penya said he would resign, for the stability of our country.

lines.text: But lawmakers refused. Resigning would have given him a lifetime Senate seat, and with it, immunity. The lower house voted 78 to 0 to impeach him instead.
lines.say: But lawmakers refused. Resigning would have given him a lifetime Senate seat, and with it, immunity. The lower house voted seventy-eight to zero to impeach him instead.

lines.text: Friday, November 6th: the Senate voted 44 to 0 to remove him. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in that evening.
lines.say: Friday, November sixth. The Senate voted forty-four to zero to remove him. Vice President Pedro Aliana was sworn in that evening.

lines.text: That night, prosecutors ordered Peña's arrest.
lines.say: That night, prosecutors ordered Penya's arrest.

lines: Over the weekend, he and the former central bank chief were charged with breach of trust. Prosecutors charged 27 people linked to the bank, and a judge ordered its founder and president detained.

lines.text: Investigators raided Peña's country house and seized luxury cars, private planes and a yacht.
lines.say: Investigators raided Penya's country house and seized luxury cars, private planes and a yacht.

lines.text: Peña denies any wrongdoing, and no one has been convicted.
lines.say: Penya denies any wrongdoing, and no one has been convicted.

lines.text: Ueno has disputed the leaked report and the reporting against it.
lines.say: Wenno has disputed the leaked report and the reporting against it.

lines: How much money is truly missing is still being counted.
This has happened before. In the late 1990s, Paraguay closed 13 banks and 35 finance companies.

lines.text: In five years, Ueno went from a small finance company to the bank in most people's pockets.
lines.say: In five years, Wenno went from a small finance company to the bank in most people's pockets.

lines.text: In five days, it took a president down with it.

lines: This story is still developing, and we'll update you as it does.
